group.title: First phrasal verbs
group.tagline: Get up, turn on, look for
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To drop to the ground.
examples: Be careful on the ice, or you’ll {fall down}.
wrong: He fell down and stayed standing.

words.meaning: To hit your foot on something and almost fall.
examples: I {tripped over} a shoe on the stairs.
wrong: She tripped over the air in an empty room.

words.meaning: To spend time at home and not go out.
examples: It’s raining, so let’s {stay in} tonight.
wrong: We stayed in and went to a club all night.

words.meaning: To enter a room or building.
examples: Please {come in} and sit down.
wrong: She came in and stayed outside the door.

words.meaning: To return to a place where you were before.
examples: I want to {go back} to Paris next year.
wrong: He went back to a place he had never been.

words.meaning: To leave a place or person.
examples: Please {go away}, I’m busy.
wrong: He went away and stayed right next to me.

words.meaning: To write the needed information on a form.
examples: {Fill out} this form with your name and address.
wrong: I filled out the form and left every box empty.

words.meaning: To do something more quickly.
examples: {Hurry up}! The train leaves in five minutes.
wrong: She hurried up and walked very slowly.

words.meaning: To put words or numbers on paper so you remember them.
examples: {Write down} my phone number.
wrong: I wrote down his name only in my head.

words.meaning: To have none of something left.
examples: We’ve {run out} of milk.
wrong: We ran out of bread, so we have lots left.

words.meaning: To stay until someone comes or something happens.
examples: I’ll {wait for} you at the station.
wrong: She waited for the bus by leaving at once.

words.meaning: To close all the doors and windows with a key.
examples: Don’t forget to {lock up} before you leave.
wrong: He locked up the house and left every door open.

words.meaning: To make a place clean and in order.
examples: Let’s {clean up} the kitchen after dinner.
wrong: We cleaned up the room by throwing food on the floor.

words.meaning: To not go into a place, or to stop something from going in.
examples: The sign said ’{Keep out}’.
wrong: Keep out means everyone is welcome to come in.

words.meaning: To move to a lower place, for example from a chair or tree.
examples: {Get down} from that table right now!
wrong: He got down from the tree by climbing higher.

words.meaning: To start living in a new home.
examples: We {moved in} last week, so there are boxes everywhere.
wrong: They moved in to the house and never lived there.

words.meaning: To leave your home and go to live somewhere else.
examples: My sister {moved out} when she was twenty.
wrong: He moved out but still lives in the same flat.

words.meaning: To move so that you face the other way.
examples: {Turn around} and look behind you.
wrong: She turned around and kept looking the same way.

words.meaning: To go somewhere with someone.
examples: We’re going to the park. Do you want to {come along}?
wrong: She came along with us by staying at home.

words.meaning: When an alarm suddenly starts to ring.
examples: My alarm {went off} at six.
wrong: The alarm went off, so the house was silent.

words.meaning: To place something you are holding on a surface.
examples: {Put down} that heavy bag and rest.
wrong: He put down the box and kept holding it.

words.meaning: To visit someone at their home.
examples: Why don’t you {come over} for dinner tonight?
wrong: She came over to my house but never visited.

words.meaning: To become higher or to rise.
examples: Prices {go up} every year.
wrong: The price went up from ten dollars to five.

words.meaning: To become lower or to fall.
examples: The temperature {went down} at night.
wrong: The number went down from three to nine.

words.meaning: To leave a place for a short time.
examples: She just {stepped out}, but she’ll be back soon.
wrong: He stepped out of the office and stayed away for a year.

words.meaning: To not know where you are or how to get somewhere.
examples: We {got lost} in the old part of the city.
wrong: I got lost, so I knew exactly where I was.

words.meaning: To return something to where it was.
examples: Please {put back} the milk when you are done.
wrong: I put back the book by taking it to my room.

words.meaning: To return something to the shop where you bought it.
examples: The shoes were too small, so I had to {take back} the pair.
wrong: I took back the shirt and kept it at home.

words.meaning: To return something to the person who owns it.
examples: Can you {give back} my pen, please?
wrong: She gave back the book and never returned it.

words.meaning: To sleep later than usual in the morning.
examples: On Sundays I {sleep in} until ten.
wrong: He slept in and got up at five, earlier than usual.

words.meaning: To get rid of something you do not want.
examples: {Throw out} those old newspapers.
wrong: I threw out the old shoes and put them back in the closet.

words.meaning: To remove something from a place.
examples: She {took out} her keys from her bag.
wrong: He took out the money and left it in his wallet.

words.meaning: To return with something.
examples: Can you {bring back} some bread from the store?
wrong: He brought back nothing, but carried a bag of bread home.

words.meaning: To visit someone for a short time without a plan.
examples: {Drop by} any time you’re near my house.
wrong: She dropped by and stayed for a whole month.

words.meaning: To connect a machine to electricity.
examples: {Plug in} the lamp next to the bed.
wrong: I plugged in the fridge to stop the electricity reaching it.

words.meaning: To move something so the other side is on top.
examples: {Turn over} the page and read the next question.
wrong: He turned over the pancake so the same side stayed on top.

words.meaning: To go past a person or place.
examples: I {pass by} the bakery on my way to school.
wrong: We passed by the shop by going inside and staying.

words.meaning: To hit something so that it falls.
examples: The cat {knocked over} my glass of water.
wrong: He knocked over the vase and it stood still.

words.meaning: To walk around a place to see what is there.
examples: We {looked around} the market before buying.
wrong: We looked around the museum with our eyes closed.

words.meaning: To choose one thing from a group.
examples: She {picked out} a red dress from the rack.
wrong: He picked out a shirt by not choosing any.
